Specify a Bayesian stochastic frontier model

Source: R/create_sfmodel.R
create_sfmodel_exp.Rd

Sets up the model object that the add_* functions operate on. The two functions differ only in the distribution assumed for the one-sided inefficiency term, which determines the class of the object and hence the methods that apply to it.

create_sfmodel_exp(
  formula,
  data,
  id = NULL,
  type = c("production", "cost"),
  iterations = 20000,
  burnin = 2000,
  thin = 1
)

create_sfmodel_hn(
  formula,
  data,
  id = NULL,
  type = c("production", "cost"),
  iterations = 20000,
  burnin = 2000,
  thin = 1
)

Arguments

formula

a model formula describing the frontier.

data

a data frame containing the variables in formula.

id

optional. Either the name of a variable in data or a vector of the same length as the data, identifying the units that own the inefficiency terms. See details.

type

either "production" or "cost".

iterations

number of iterations retained after burn-in, before thinning.

burnin

number of discarded iterations.

thin

thinning interval. iterations must be a multiple of it.

Value

An object of class "sfmodel_exp" or "sfmodel_hn", both inheriting from "sfmodel". Rows with a missing value in the model frame, or with an unknown unit, are dropped with a message and recorded in the element na.action. An offset in the formula is subtracted from the response and kept as data$offset, so data$y is the response the sampler sees rather than the one supplied.

Details

The model is $$y_i = x_i' \beta - u_{g(i)} + v_i, \quad v_i \sim N(0, \sigma_v^2),$$ for a production frontier, with the sign of \(u\) reversed for a cost frontier. The frontier \(x_i'\beta\) is the maximum output attainable with the inputs \(x_i\), and \(\exp(-u_i)\) the efficiency with which unit \(i\) reaches it.

The response is assumed to be on a logarithmic scale, and the regressors usually are as well. That is what makes \(\exp(-u_i)\) an efficiency: \(u_i\) is then a proportional shortfall, so a unit with \(u_i = 0.1\) produces about ten per cent less than its inputs allow. Fitting output in levels does not merely change the units of \(u\), it changes the answer, because the prior on the inefficiency term is expressed in the units of the response: the same data measured in euros and in millions of euros give different efficiency scores. See add_priors.

create_sfmodel_exp assumes \(u \sim Exp(\lambda)\) and create_sfmodel_hn assumes \(u \sim N^+(0, \sigma_u^2)\). The choice matters mainly for the prior, since the exponential model admits an exact elicitation from a prior median efficiency; see add_priors.

A term wrapped in offset enters the frontier with its coefficient fixed at one, as it does in lm. This is how a known quantity is imposed rather than estimated: a capacity that the frontier cannot exceed, or a scale factor whose elasticity is known to be one. The efficiency scores are measured from the frontier including it.

If id is supplied, one inefficiency term is drawn per unit and held fixed over that unit's observations, which is the time-invariant panel model of Pitt and Lee (1981). This attributes all persistent heterogeneity between units to inefficiency, and is therefore a strong assumption whenever units differ systematically for reasons unrelated to efficiency. Leaving id at NULL gives every observation its own inefficiency term.

References

Pitt, M. M., & Lee, L.-F. (1981). The measurement and sources of technical inefficiency in the Indonesian weaving industry. Journal of Development Economics, 9(1), 43–64.

See also

add_priors, add_initial_values, add_seed, add_posterior_coefficients, skewness_test

Examples

set.seed(1234)
d <- sim_sf(n = 200, beta = c(1, 0.5, 0.3), sigma_v = 0.2, par_u = 4)

model <- create_sfmodel_exp(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d,
                            iterations = 500, burnin = 200)
model
#> Bayesian stochastic frontier model
#> 
#> Frontier:           production
#> Inefficiency:       exponential
#> Observations:       200
#> Coefficients:       3
#> Inefficiency terms: 200 (one per observation)
#> Iterations:         500 after 200 burn-in, thinning 1
#> 
#> Specification:
#>   priors         not set
#>   initial values not set
#>   seed           not set
#>   posterior      not simulated
